## Packages {.sparse-slide}

Load the standard packages and new package `modelbased`.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| label: load

# install.packages("marginaleffects") # needed for modelbased
# install.packages("modelbased")

library(tidyverse) 
library(haven) # not core tidyverse
library(gssr)
library(gssrdoc)
library(summarytools)
library(gtsummary) 
library(modelbased)

# do not load moderndive(), use it specifically 

```

## Load your data {.sparse-slide}

```{r}
#| message: false
#| label: gssdata

# Load all gss
gss24 <- gss_get_yr(2024)

```

## Variables {.sparse-slide .smaller}

- `year` Survey year
- `tvhours` Hours per day watching tv
- `realrinc` R's income in constant \$
- `age` Age of respondent
- `educ` Respondents highest edu credit
- `hrs1` How many hours did you work last week
- `childs` How many children have you ever had?
- `polviews` Think of self as liberal or conservative
- `sex` Respondents sex
- `marital` R's marital status

##  {.smaller data-menu-title="Variable Management"}

::: task
{{< fa check-double >}} Make a df with only the (pretty) categorical and
continuous variables we'll analyze.
:::

```{r}
#| message: false
#| label: my-data

# Categorical Variables
my_cat <- gss24 |>
  select(id, year, polviews, sex, marital) |>
  zap_missing() |>
  mutate(
    polviews = as_factor(polviews),
    sex = as_factor(sex),
    marital = as_factor(marital)) |> 
  droplevels()

# Continuous Variables
my_con <- gss24 |>
  select(id, year, tvhours, age, educ, hrs1, realrinc, childs) |>
  mutate(
    age = as.numeric(age),
    educ = as.numeric(educ),
    hrs1 = as.numeric(hrs1),
    realrinc = as.numeric(realrinc),
    childs = as.numeric(childs))

# Combine the two dataframes
my_data <- full_join(my_cat, my_con, by = c("year", "id")) |> # match by 2 vars
  drop_na()
```

# Predictions {.theme-section}

##  {data-menu-title="Regression Model"}

OLS Regression Predicting Annual Income

```{r}
#| label: regress-03
#| echo: false

model <- lm(formula = realrinc ~ hrs1 + educ + sex + marital, data = my_data)

model |>
    tbl_regression(
    intercept = TRUE,
        show_single_row = sex,
    label = list(
      sex = "Women",
      marital = "Marital status (ref. = married)")) |>
  remove_row_type(type = c("reference")) |>  
  modify_column_hide(conf.low) |>
  modify_column_unhide(
    column = std.error) |>
  remove_abbreviation() |>
  add_significance_stars() |>
  add_glance_table(
    include = c("r.squared", "nobs"))

```

## Typical-person predictions {.smaller .sparse-slide}

[**What does "holding other variables constant"
mean?**]{style="color: #3498db; font-size: 125%; font-family: 'Shadows Into Light'"}

<br>

For a prediction at the means, we set:  
  
-    continuous variables to their means  
-    categorical variables to their reference categories

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: means

mean(my_data$hrs1)
mean(my_data$educ)

```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Hours worked = 39.56\
Education = 14.80\
Sex = Male (reference)\
Marital status = Married (reference)
:::
:::::

## Typical-person predictions {.sparse-slide}

```{r}
#| label: typical

estimate_means(
  model,
  estimate = "typical")
```

##  {.sparse-slide data-menu-title="Typical-person predictions"}

```{r}
#| label: typical-ggplot
#| echo: false

preds <- estimate_means(
  model,
  estimate = "typical")

ggplot(
  preds,
  aes(x = marital, y = Mean, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(size = 3,
             position = position_dodge(width = .4)) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = CI_low, ymax = CI_high),
    width = .1,
    position = position_dodge(width = .4)) +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted Income for Typical People",
    subtitle = "Hours worked and education fixed at their means",
    x = "Marital Status",
    y = "Predicted Income",
    color = "Gender") +
  theme_minimal(20)
```

## Marginal Means {.sparse-slide .smaller}

**Marginal means are adjusted group averages**.\
Calculated from the regression model while accounting for the distribution of the other predictors in the data.  

<br>

```{r}
#| label: typical-sex

marginal_means <- estimate_means(
  model,
  by = "sex",
  estimate = "typical")

marginal_means
```

## Average Adjusted Predictions (AAP) {.sparse-slide .smaller}

**Average adjusted predictions are adjusted population averages.**\
Calculated from the regression model using the actual characteristics of individuals in the dataset.  

```{r}
#| label: aap-sex

aap <- estimate_means(
  model,
  by = "sex",
  estimate = "average")

aap

```

::: notes
Unlike a typical-person prediction, AAPs do not create a hypothetical "average" person. Instead, predictions are generated using the observed characteristics of individuals in the dataset and then averaged.
:::  


##  {.smaller .sparse-slide data-menu-title="Marginal Means & AAP"}

```{r}
#| label: compare
#| echo: false

marginal_means$method <- "Marginal Means"
aap$method <- "AAP"

bind_rows(marginal_means, aap) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(x = sex, y = Mean,
        color = method,
        group = method)) +
  geom_point(size = 4,
             position = position_dodge(width = .4)) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = CI_low, ymax = CI_high),
    position = position_dodge(width = .4),
    width = .1) +
  labs(
    title = "Marginal Means vs. Average Adjusted Predictions",
    subtitle = "Predicted income for men and women",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Predicted Income",
    color = "Method"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20)
```

## Three Types of Predictions {.sparse-slide}

**Typical-person prediction**  
Prediction for a hypothetical person with average values.  

<br>

**Marginal mean**
Adjusted average prediction for a group.

<br>

**Average adjusted prediction (AAP)**
Adjusted average prediction calculated using the actual characteristics of people in the data.

##  {data-menu-title="Code Meets Question" .sparse-slide background-image="images/gears-solid-full.png" background-size="80px" background-repeat="repeat"}

::: task
{{< fa lightbulb >}} Does the relationship between hours worked and income depend on education?
:::


```{r}
#| label: regress-03
#| echo: false

model <- lm(formula = realrinc ~ hrs1 + educ + sex + marital, data = my_data)

# Predicted income across levels of education
estimate_means(model, by = "educ")
estimate_means(model, by = "educ = c(12, 16, 18, 20)")

# Across hours worked
estimate_means(model, by = "hrs1")


model_int <- lm(realrinc ~ hrs1 * educ + sex + marital, data = my_data)

# educ at selected values, hrs1 at selected values
estimate_means(model_int, by = c("educ = c(10, 12, 16)", "hrs1 = c(20, 40, 60)"))

```













# Old slides

## `estimate_means()` {.sparse-slide}

```{r}
#| label: estimate_means_margins
#| output-location: fragment

# Get predicted values
preds <- estimate_means(model, by = c("sex"))

# Preview the new df
preds |>
  as_tibble() |> 
  head()
```

::: notes
R calculates the mean values of every variable in the model except sex,
and sets all of those variables equal to their means. Then (once again)
it sets female = 0 in every observation, calculates predicted
probabilities for each individual, and averages those.

Then it goes back and resets female to 1 in every observation, again
calculates predicted probabilities for each individual and outputs the
average of those.

Outputs can be interpreted as the predicted probabilities for women and
men if they were all average in all other respects.
:::

## `estimate_means()` {.sparse-slide}

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#| label: estimate_means_code

# Get predicted values
preds <- estimate_means(model, by = c("educ", "sex"))

# Preview the new df
preds |>
  as_tibble() |> 
  head()
```

# Interactions

##  {.sparse-slide data-menu-title="Code Meets Question" background-image="images/gears-solid-full.png" background-size="80px" background-repeat="repeat"}

::: task
{{< fa lightbulb >}} Does the relationship between TV hours and
education differ by political identity?
:::

<br>

. . .

```{r}
#| label: regress-06

my_data <- my_data |>
  mutate(pol_group = case_when(
    polviews %in% c("extremely liberal", "liberal", "slightly liberal") ~ "Liberal",
    polviews == "moderate, middle of the road" ~ "Moderate",
    polviews %in% c("slightly conservative", "conservative", "extremely conservative") ~ "Conservative",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_))

model <- lm(tvhours ~ educ * pol_group, data = my_data)

moderndive::get_regression_table(model)
```

::: notes
The coefficient for `educ` is \$-0.142 \$, meaning that for moderates
(the reference group), each additional year of education is associated
with -0.142 fewer tv hours per day.

The coefficient for `pol_group: Conservative` is $-0.1$. This is the
difference in the outcome between moderates and conservatives when
education = 0. Conservatives watch -0.1 TV hours per day fewer than
moderates when education is zero. Not statistically significantly
different.

The interaction term `educ:pol_groupConservative` is $-0.008$. It tells
us whether the relationship between education and TV hours differs
between moderates and conservatives It adjusts the slope of education
for conservatives So for conservatives, the effect of education is:

$-0.142 -0.008 = -0.15$

This means that for conservatives, each additional unit of education is
associated with only $-0.15$ fewer daily TV hours.
:::

##  {.sparse-slide data-menu-title="`ggplot()`"}

```{r}
#| label: ggplot-interaction
#| output-location: slide

# Get predicted values
preds <- estimate_means(model, by = c("educ", "pol_group"))

# Plot using ggplot2
preds |>
  ggplot(aes(x = educ, y = Mean, color = pol_group)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
    labs(
      title = "Predicted Daily TV Hours by Education and Political Identity",
      x = "Education Level",
      y = "Predicted TV Hours",
      color = "Political Identity") +
    theme_minimal(20) +
    theme(legend.position = "top")
```
